entries.ee41cef8646ad3e7fdec5ece10005d36a95fead7: <div sID="gen17662" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Jer.21" sID="Jer.21"/> <div eID="gen17662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17663" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17664" type="x-p"/> It is plain that the prophecies of this book are not placed here in the same order in which they were preached; for there are chapters after this which concern Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah, who all reigned before Zedekiah, in whose reign the prophecy of this chapter bears date. Here is, I. The message which Zedekiah sent to the prophet, to desire him to enquire of the Lord for them, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1-Jer.21.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The answer which Jeremiah, in God's name, sent to that message, in which, 1. He foretels the certain and inevitable ruin of the city, and the fruitlessness of their attempts for its preservation, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.3-Jer.21.7">ver. 3-7</reference>. 2. He advises the people to make the best of bad, by going over to the king of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.8-Jer.21.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 3. He advises the king and his family to repent and reform (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.11-Jer.21.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>), and not to trust to the strength of their city and grow secure, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13-Jer.21.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>.
entries.18b022358af86b3d090719a6dc90db0702ab2668: <div eID="gen17664" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17663" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Zedekiah's Message to Jeremiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen17665" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word which came unto Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when king Zedekiah sent unto him Pashur the son of Melchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Enquire, I pray thee, of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for us; for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon maketh war against us; if so be that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will deal with us according to all his wondrous works, that he may go up from us. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then said Jeremiah unto them, Thus shall ye say to Zedekiah: <hi type="super">4</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel; Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in your hands, wherewith ye fight against the king of Babylon, and <hi type="italic">against</hi> the Chaldeans, which besiege you without the walls, and I will assemble them into the midst of this city. <hi type="super">5</hi> And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I will smite the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast: they shall die of a great pestilence. <hi type="super">7</hi> And afterward, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, and his servants, and the people, and such as are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those that seek their life: and he shall smite them with the edge of the sword; he shall not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy. <div eID="gen17665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17666" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A very humble decent message which king Zedekiah, when he was in distress, sent to Jeremiah the prophet. It is indeed charged upon this Zedekiah that he <hi type="italic">humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet, speaking from the mouth of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.12">2 Chron. xxxvi. 12</reference>); he did not always humble himself as he did sometimes; he never humbled himself till necessity forced him to it; he humbled himself so far as to desire the prophet's assistance, but not so far as to take his advice, or to be ruled by him. Observe, <div eID="gen17666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17667" type="x-p"/> 1. The distress which king Zedekiah was now in: <hi type="italic">Nebuchadrezzar made war upon him,</hi> not only invaded the land, but besieged the city, and had now actually invested it. Note, Those that put the evil day far from them will be the more terrified when it comes upon them; and those who before slighted God's ministers may then perhaps be glad to court an acquaintance with them. <div eID="gen17667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17668" type="x-p"/> 2. The messengers he sent—<hi type="italic">Pashur and Zephaniah,</hi> one belonging to the fifth course of the priests, the other to the twenty-fourth, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.9">1 Chron. xxiv. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.18">18</reference>. It was well that he sent, and that he sent persons of rank; but it would have been better if he had desired a personal conference with the prophet, which no doubt he might easily have had if he would so far have humbled himself. Perhaps these priests were no better than the rest, and yet, when they were commanded by the king, they must carry a respectful message to the prophet, which was both a mortification to them and an honour to Jeremiah. He had rashly said (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.18">ch. xx. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">My days are consumed with shame;</hi> and yet here we find that he lived to see better days than those were when he made that complaint; now he appears in reputation. Note, It is folly to say, when things are bad with us, "They will always be so." It is possible that those who are despised may come to be respected; and it is promised that those who <hi type="italic">honour God he will honour,</hi> and that those who have <hi type="italic">afflicted his people shall bow to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.60.14">Isa. lx. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen17668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17669" type="x-p"/> 3. The message itself: <hi type="italic">Enquire, I pray thee, of the Lord for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">v. 2</reference>. Now that the Chaldean army had got into their borders, into their bowels, they were at length convinced that Jeremiah was a true prophet, though loth to own it and brought too late to it. Under this conviction they desire him to stand their friend with God, believing him to have that interest in heaven which none of their other prophets had, who had flattered them with hopes of peace. They now employ Jeremiah, (1.) To consult the mind of God for them: "<hi type="italic">Enquire of the Lord for us;</hi> ask him what course we shall take in our present strait, for the measures we have hitherto taken are all broken." Note, Those that will not take the direction of God's grace how to get clear of their sins would yet be glad of the directions of his providence how to get clear of their troubles. (2.) To seek the favour of God for them (so some read it): "<hi type="italic">Entreat the Lord for us;</hi> be an intercessor for us with God." Note, Those that slight the prayers of God's people and ministers when they are in prosperity may perhaps be glad of an interest in them when they come to be in distress. <hi type="italic">Give us of your oil.</hi> The benefit they promise themselves is, <hi type="italic">It may be the Lord will deal with us</hi> now <hi type="italic">according to the wondrous works he wrought for our fathers,</hi> that the enemy may raise the siege and <hi type="italic">go up from us.</hi> Observe, [1.] All their care is to get rid of their trouble, not to make their peace with God and be reconciled to him—"That our enemy may <hi type="italic">go up from us,</hi>" not, "That our God may return to us." Thus Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.17">Exod. x. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Entreat the Lord that he may take away this death.</hi> [2.] All their hope is that God had done wondrous works formerly in the deliverance of Jerusalem when Sennacherib besieged it, at the prayer of Isaiah (so we are told, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.20-2Chr.32.21">2 Chron. xxxii. 20, 21</reference>), and who can tell but he may destroy these besiegers (as he did those) at the prayer of Jeremiah? But they did not consider how different the character of Zedekiah and his people was from that of Hezekiah and his people: those were days of general reformation and piety, these of general corruption and apostasy. Jerusalem is now the reverse of what it was then. Note, It is folly to think that God should do for us while we hold fast our iniquity as he did for those that held fast their integrity. <div eID="gen17669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17670" type="x-p"/> II. A very startling cutting reply which God, by the prophet, sent to that message. If Jeremiah had been to have answered the message of himself we have reason to think that he would have returned a comfortable answer, in hope that their sending such a message was an indication of some good purposes in them, which he would be glad to make the best of, for he did not desire the woeful day. But God knows their hearts better than Jeremiah does, and sends them an answer which has scarcely one word of comfort in it. He sends it to them in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord God of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.3">v. 3</reference>), to intimate to them that though God allowed himself to be called the <hi type="italic">God of Israel,</hi> and had done great things for Israel formerly, and had still great things in store for Israel, pursuant to his covenants with them, yet this should stand the present generation in no stead, who were Israelites in name only, and not in deed, any more than God's dealings with them should cut off his relation to Israel as their God. It is here foretold, <div eID="gen17670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17671" type="x-p"/> 1. That God will render all their endeavours for their own security fruitless and ineffectual (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">v. 4</reference>): "I will be so far from teaching your hands to war, and putting an edge upon your swords, that I will <hi type="italic">turn back the weapons of war that are in your hand,</hi> when you sally out upon the besiegers to beat them off, so that they shall not give the stroke you design; nay, they shall recoil into your own faces, and be turned upon yourselves." Nothing can make for those who have God against them. <div eID="gen17671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17672" type="x-p"/> 2. That the besiegers shall in a little time make themselves masters of Jerusalem, and of all its wealth and strength: <hi type="italic">I will assemble</hi> those <hi type="italic">in the midst of this city</hi> who are now surrounding it. Note, If that place which should have been a centre of devotion be made a centre of wickedness, it is not strange if God make it a rendezvous of destroyers. <div eID="gen17672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17673" type="x-p"/> 3. That God himself will be their enemy; and then I know not who can befriend them, no, not Jeremiah himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.5">v. 5</reference>): "I will be so far from protecting you, as I have done formerly in a like case, that <hi type="italic">I myself will fight against you.</hi>" Note, Those who rebel against God may justly expect that he will make war upon them, and that, (1.) With the power of a God who is irresistibly victorious: <hi type="italic">I will fight against you with an outstretched hand,</hi> which will reach far, and <hi type="italic">with a strong arm,</hi> which will strike home and wound deeply. (2.) With the displeasure of a God who is indisputably righteous. It is not a correction in love, but an execution <hi type="italic">in anger, in fury, and in great wrath;</hi> it is upon a sentence sworn in wrath, against which there will lie no exception, and it will soon be found what a fearful thing it is to fall into the hands of the living God. <div eID="gen17673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17674" type="x-p"/> 4. That those who, for their own safety, decline sallying out upon the besiegers, and so avoid their sword, shall yet not escape the sword of God's justice (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will smite those that abide in the city</hi> (so it may be read), <hi type="italic">both man and beast,</hi> both the beasts that are for food and those that are for service in war, foot and horse; <hi type="italic">they shall, die of a great pestilence,</hi> which shall rage within the walls, while the enemies are encamped about them. Though Jerusalem's gates and walls may for a time keep out the Chaldeans, they cannot keep out God's judgments. His arrows of pestilence can reach those that think themselves safe from other arrows. <div eID="gen17674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17675" type="x-p"/> 5. That the king himself, and people that escape the <hi type="italic">sword, famine,</hi> and <hi type="italic">pestilence,</hi> shall fall <hi type="italic">into the hands</hi> of the Chaldeans, who shall cut them off in cold blood (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">v. 7</reference>): They <hi type="italic">shall not spare them,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">have pity</hi> on them. Let not those expect to find mercy with men who have forfeited God's compassions, and shut themselves out from his mercy. Thus had the decree gone forth; and then to what purpose was it for Jeremiah to <hi type="italic">enquire of the Lord for them?</hi>
entries.fd753a9c0fafea0b9e66f66a30a0bd6da217f3b8: <div eID="gen17675" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Answer to Zedekiah's Message; Advice to the King and the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 590.)</title> <div sID="gen17676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And unto this people thou shalt say, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death. <hi type="super">9</hi> He that abideth in this city shall die by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence: but he that goeth out, and falleth to the Chaldeans that besiege you, he shall live, and his life shall be unto him for a prey. <hi type="super">10</hi> For I have set my face against this city for evil, and not for good, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire. <hi type="super">11</hi> And touching the house of the king of Judah, <hi type="italic">say,</hi> Hear ye the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="super">12</hi> O house of David, thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Execute judgment in the morning, and deliver <hi type="italic">him that is</hi> spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, lest my fury go out like fire, and burn that none can quench <hi type="italic">it,</hi> because of the evil of your doings. <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, O inhabitant of the valley, <hi type="italic">and</hi> rock of the plain, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; which say, Who shall come down against us? or who shall enter into our habitations? <hi type="super">14</hi> But I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and I will kindle a fire in the forest thereof, and it shall devour all things round about it. <div eID="gen17676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> By the civil message which the king sent to Jeremiah it appeared that both he and the people began to have a respect for him, which it would have been Jeremiah's policy to make some advantage of for himself; but the reply which God obliges him to make is enough to crush the little respect they begin to have for him, and to exasperate them against him more than ever. Not only the predictions in the <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1-Jer.21.7">foregoing verses</reference>, but the prescriptions in these, were provoking; for here, <div eID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17678" type="x-p"/> I. He advises the people to surrender and desert to the Chaldeans, as the only means left them to save their lives, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.8-Jer.21.10">v. 8-10</reference>. This counsel was very displeasing to those who were flattered by their false prophets into a desperate resolution to hold out to the last extremity, trusting to the strength of their walls and the courage of their soldiery to keep out the enemy, or to their foreign aids to raise the siege. The prophet assures them, "<hi type="italic">The city shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon,</hi> and he shall not only plunder it, but <hi type="italic">burn it with fire,</hi> for God himself hath <hi type="italic">set his face against this city for evil and not for good,</hi> to lay it waste and not to protect it, <hi type="italic">for evil</hi> which shall have no good mixed with it, no mitigation or merciful allay; and therefore, if you would make the best of bad, you must beg quarter of the Chaldeans, and surrender prisoners of war." In vain did Rabshakeh persuade the Jews to do this while they had God for them (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.16">Isa. xxxvi. 16</reference>), but it was the best course they could take now that God was against them. Both the law and the prophets had often set before them life and death in another sense—life if they obey the voice of God, death if they persist in disobedience, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.19">Deut. xxx. 19</reference>. But they had slighted that life which would have made them truly happy, to upbraid them with which the prophet here uses the same expression (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death,</hi> which denotes not, as that, a fair proposal, but a melancholy dilemma, advising them of two evils to choose the less; and that less evil, a shameful and wretched captivity, is all the life now left for them to propose to themselves. <hi type="italic">He that abides in the city,</hi> and trusts to that to secure him, shall certainly die either by <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> without the walls or <hi type="italic">famine</hi> or <hi type="italic">pestilence</hi> within. But he that can so far bring down his spirit, and quit his vain hopes, as to go out, and fall <hi type="italic">to the Chaldeans, his life shall be given him for a prey;</hi> he shall save his life, but with much difficulty and hazard, as a prey is taken from the mighty. It is an expression like that, <hi type="italic">He shall be saved, yet so as by fire.</hi> He shall escape but very narrowly, or he shall have such surprising joy and satisfaction in escaping with his life from such a universal destruction as shall equal theirs that divide the spoil. They thought to make a prey of the camp of the Chaldeans, as their ancestors did that of the Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.23">Isa. xxxiii. 23</reference>), but they will be sadly disappointed; if by yielding at discretion they can but save their lives, that is all the prey they must promise themselves. Now one would think this advice from a prophet, in God's name, should have gained some credit with them and been universally followed; but, for aught that appears, there were few or none that took it; so wretchedly were their hearts hardened, to their destruction. <div eID="gen17678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> II. He advises the king and princes to reform, and make conscience of the duty of their place. Because it was the king that sent the message to him, in the reply there shall be a particular word for <hi type="italic">the house of the king,</hi> not to compliment or court them (that was no part of the prophet's business, no, not when they did him the honour to send to him), but to give them wholesome counsel (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.11-Jer.21.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Execute judgment in the morning;</hi> do it carefully and diligently. Those magistrates that would fill up their place with duty had need rise betimes. Do it quickly, and do not delay to do justice upon appeals made to you, and tire out poor petitioners as you have done. Do not lie in your beds in a morning to sleep away the debauch of the night before, nor spend the morning in pampering the body (as those princes, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Eccl. x. 16</reference>), but spend it in the despatch of business. You would be delivered out of the hand of those that distress you, and expect that therein God should do you justice; see then that you do justice to those that apply to you, and <hi type="italic">deliver them out of the hand of their oppressors, lest my fury go out like fire</hi> against you in a particular manner, and you fare worst who think to escape best, <hi type="italic">because of the evil of your doings.</hi>" Now, 1. This intimates that it was their neglect to do their duty that brought all this desolation upon the people. It was the <hi type="italic">evil of their doings</hi> that kindled the fire of God's wrath. Thus plainly does he deal even with the <hi type="italic">house of the king;</hi> for those that would have the benefit of a prophet's prayers must thankfully take a prophet's reproofs. 2. This directs them to take the right method for a national reformation. The princes must begin, and set a good example, and then the people will be invited to reform. They must use their power for the punishment of wrong, and then the people will be obliged to reform. He reminds them that they are <hi type="italic">the house of David,</hi> and therefore should tread in his steps, who executed judgment and justice to his people. 3. This gives them some encouragement to hope that there may yet be a lengthening of their tranquillity, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Dan. iv. 27</reference>. If any thing will recover their state from the brink of ruin, this will. <div eID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17680" type="x-p"/> III. He shows them the vanity of all their hopes so long as they continued unreformed, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13-Jer.21.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Jerusalem is an <hi type="italic">inhabitant of the valley,</hi> guarded with mountains on all sides, which were their natural fortifications, making it difficult for an army to approach them. It is a <hi type="italic">rock of the plain,</hi> which made it difficult for an enemy to undermine them. These advantages of their situation they trusted to more than to the power and promise of God; and, thinking their city by these means to be impregnable, they set the judgments of God at defiance, saying, "<hi type="italic">Who shall come down against us?</hi> None of our neighbours dare make a descent upon us, or, if they do, <hi type="italic">who shall enter into our habitations?</hi>" They had some colour for this confidence; for it appears to have been the sense of all their neighbours that no enemy could force his way into Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.12">Lam. iv. 12</reference>. But those are least safe that are most secure. God soon shows the vanity of that challenge, <hi type="italic">Who shall come down against us?</hi> when he says (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold, I am against thee.</hi> They had indeed by the wickedness driven God out of their city when he would have tarried with them as a friend; but they could not by their bulwarks keep them out of their city when he came against them as an enemy. If God be for us, who can be against us? But, if he be against us, who can be for us, to stand us in any stead? Nay, he comes against them not as an enemy that may lawfully and with some hope of success be resisted, but as a judge that cannot be resisted; for he says (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will punish you,</hi> by due course of law, <hi type="italic">according to the fruit of your doings,</hi> that is, according to the merit of them and the direct tendency of them. That shall be brought upon you which is the natural product of sin. Nay, he will not only come with the anger of an enemy and the justice of a judge, but with the force of a consuming fire, which has no compassion, as a judge sometimes has, nor spares any thing combustible that comes in its way. Jerusalem has become a forest, in which God will <hi type="italic">kindle a fire</hi> that shall consume all before it; for our God is himself <hi type="italic">a consuming fire;</hi> and <hi type="italic">who is able to stand in his sight</hi> when once he is angry?  <chapter eID="Jer.21"/> <div eID="gen17680" type="x-p"/>

entries.dd3e0d718451a8136b521b5708292c5b972f09cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10040"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 21</title> <title type="x-s3">Jr 21:1-44. Zedekiah Consults Jeremiah What Is to Be the Event of the War: God's Answer.</title> <div sID="gen17888" type="x-p"/> Written probably when, after having repulsed the Egyptians who brought succors to the Jews (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5-Jer.37.8">Jr 37:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>), the Chaldees were a second time advancing against Jerusalem, but were not yet closely besieging it (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jr 21:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">13</reference>) [Rosenmuller]. This chapter probably ought to be placed between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eight chapters; since what the "princes," in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>, represent Jeremiah as having said, is exactly what we find in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jr 21:9</reference>. Moreover, the same persons as here (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>) are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">38:1</reference>, namely, Pashur and Zephaniah. What is here more fully related is there simply referred to in the historical narrative. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24">Jr 52:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2Ki 25:18</reference> [Maurer].<div eID="gen17888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10040"/><hi type="bold">1. Zedekiah--</hi>a prince having some reverence for sacred things, for which reason he sends an honorable embassy to Jeremiah; but not having moral courage to obey his better impulses.<div eID="gen17889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pashur--</hi>son of Melchiah, of the fifth order of priests, distinct from Pashur, son of Immer (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.1">Jr 20:1</reference>), of the sixteenth order (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.9">1Ch 24:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen17890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zephaniah--</hi>of the twenty-fourth order. They are designated, not by their father, but by their family (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.18">1Ch 24:18</reference>). <div eID="gen17891" type="x-p"/>
entries.aeefd18da0742e3329df1d231e5169720b068479: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10041"/><div sID="gen17892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10041"/><hi type="bold">2. Nebuchadrezzar--</hi>the more usual way of spelling the name in Jeremiah than Nebuchadnezzar. From Persiac roots, meaning either "Nebo, the chief of the gods," or, "Nebo, the god of fire." He was son of Nabopolassar, who committed the command of the army against Egypt, at Carchemish, and against Judea, to the crown prince.<div eID="gen17892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to all his wondrous works--</hi>Zedekiah hopes for God's special interposition, such as was vouchsafed to Hezekiah against Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">36</reference>).<div eID="gen17893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen17894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go up from us--</hi>rise up from the siege which he sat down to lay (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.11">11</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Num.16.24">Nu 16:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.19">1Ki 15:19</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen17895" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cd39a25f1776251d4202c65870333627a8ad572: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10042"/><div sID="gen17896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10042"/><hi type="bold">4. God of Israel--</hi>Those "wondrous works" (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jr 21:2</reference>) do not belong to you; God is faithful; it is you who forfeit the privileges of the covenant by unfaithfulness. "God will always remain the God of Israel, though He destroy thee and thy people" [Calvin].<div eID="gen17896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn back the weapons--</hi>I will turn them to a very different use from what you intend them. With them you now fight against the Chaldees "without the walls" (the Jewish defenders being as yet able to sally forth more freely, and defend the fountains outside the walls in the valley under Mount Zion; see <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jr 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.6">Jr 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">7</reference>); but soon ye shall be driven back within the city [Maurer], and "in the midst" of it, I will cause all your arms to be gathered in one place ("I will assemble them," namely, your arms) by the Chaldean conquerors [Grotius], who shall slay you with those very arms [Menochius]. <div eID="gen17897" type="x-p"/>
entries.09044aded7b45a0b8384c4857debcdcf8fdaa5f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10043"/><div sID="gen17898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10043"/>5. The Jews shall have not merely the Chaldees, but Jehovah Himself in wrath at their provocations, fighting against them. Every word enhances the formidable character of God's opposition, "I myself ... outstretched hand ... strong arm (no longer as in <reference osisRef="Exod.6.6">Ex 6:6</reference>, and in the case of Sennacherib, in your behalf, but) in anger ... fury ... great wrath." <div eID="gen17898" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3725a1fcbda0931b147497b1896bf0bdc5f1ca1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10044"/><div sID="gen17899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10044"/><hi type="bold">7. the people, and such--</hi>rather, explanatory, "the people," namely, "such as are left."<div eID="gen17899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek their life--</hi>content with nothing short of their death; not content with plundering and enslaving them.<div eID="gen17900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smite with ... sword--</hi>This was the fate of Zedekiah's sons and many of the Jewish nobles. Zedekiah himself, though not put to a violent death, died of grief. Compare as to the accurate fulfilment, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">Jr 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.6">2Ki 25:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.7">7</reference>. <div eID="gen17901" type="x-p"/>
entries.14ceccc03a43bee93927cb161ca3f6730ce478de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10045"/><div sID="gen17902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10045"/>8. "Life," if ye surrender; "death," if ye persist in opposing the Chaldees (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.30.19">De 30:19</reference>). The individuality of Jeremiah's mission from God is shown in that he urges to unconditional surrender; whereas all former prophets had urged the people to oppose their invaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">Is 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.33">37:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">35</reference>). <div eID="gen17902" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a0bdec4d58fe75958aa6aa2c88cb072aa5af7ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10046"/><div sID="gen17903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10046"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.18">17, 18</reference>).<div eID="gen17903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">falleth to--</hi>deserts to.<div eID="gen17904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">life ... a prey--</hi>proverbial, to make one's escape with life, like a valuable spoil or prey that one carries off; the narrowness of the escape, and the joy felt at it, are included in the idea (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.18">Jr 39:18</reference>). <div eID="gen17905" type="x-p"/>
entries.206412a57f0454631a64c7787ecd36d20e55448e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10047"/><div sID="gen17906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10047"/><hi type="bold">10. set ... face against--</hi>determined to punish (See on <reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Le 17:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17906" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe5dadf75cb180e394f2f6bfa215d0960f049d58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10048"/><div sID="gen17907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10048"/><hi type="bold">12. house of David--</hi>the royal family and all in office about the king. He calls them so, because it was the greater disgrace that they had so degenerated from the piety of their forefather, David; and to repress their glorying in their descent from him, as if they were therefore inviolable; but God will not spare them as apostates.<div eID="gen17907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the morning--</hi>alluding to the time of dispensing justice (<reference osisRef="Job.24.17">Job 24:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">Psa 101:8</reference>); but the sense is mainly proverbial, for "with promptness" (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">143:8</reference>). Maurer translates, "every morning."<div eID="gen17908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest my fury ... like fire--</hi>Already it was kindled, and the decree of God gone forth against the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jr 21:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.5">5</reference>), but the king and his house may yet be preserved by repentance and reformation. God urges to righteousness, not as if they can thereby escape punishment wholly, but as the condition of a mitigation of it. <div eID="gen17909" type="x-p"/>
entries.1940f7d9feebe51e3e25424b602e0c847ac2eb4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10049"/><div sID="gen17910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10049"/><hi type="bold">13. inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain--</hi>Jerusalem personified; situated for the most part on hills, with valleys at the bottom of them, as the valley of Hinnom, &c.; and beyond the valleys and mountains again, a position most fortified by nature, whence the inhabitants fancied themselves beyond the reach of enemies; but since God is "against" them, their position will avail nothing for them. The "valley" between Mount Zion and Moriah is called Tyropoeon. Robinson takes, "rock of the plain" as Mount Zion, on which is a level tract of some extent. It is appropriately here referred to, being the site of the royal residence of the "house of David," addressed (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>). <div eID="gen17910" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcd0a6003b10d03f1c8ce64c3eb8dbd43e7af165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10050"/><div sID="gen17911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10050"/><hi type="bold">14. fruit of your doings--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Is 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen17911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest thereof--</hi>namely of your city, taken from <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jr 21:13</reference>. "Forest" refers to the dense mass of houses built of cedar, &c., brought from Lebanon (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.7">Jr 22:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.13">52:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.9">2Ki 25:9</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.21"/>

entries.249027d90d2c157ea9756093976cb892533e5d50: <div eID="gen29817" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29818" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29819" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29819" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29818" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29820" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar being come up against Jerusalem, Zedekiah sends Pashur and Zephaniah to the prophet to request him to intercede with God in behalf of his people, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jer 21:2</reference>. But he is declared to be against Jerusalem, and the whole land of Judah; and the only mitigation of their punishment must proceed from their surrendering to the king of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.3-Jer.21.10">Jer 21:3-10</reference>. Prophecy concerning the house of the king of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.11">Jer 21:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jer 21:12</reference>. Notwithstanding the amazing fortifications round about Jerusalem, in which the people vainly trust, the Lord will most assuredly visit them for their iniquities; the city shall be taken by the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jer 21:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.14">Jer 21:14</reference>. <div eID="gen29820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29821" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29822" type="x-p"/> The word which came unto Jeremiah - The chapters in the remaining parts of this prophecy seem strangely interchanged. This subject has been mentioned in the introduction, and some tables given; and to these the critical reader is requested to refer. The discourse here was delivered about the ninth year or the reign of Zedekiah. This chapter, observes Dr. Blayney, contains the first of those prophecies which were delivered by Jeremiah, subsequent to the revolt of Zedekiah, and the breaking out of the war thereupon; and which are continued on to the taking of Jerusalem, related in chap. 29, in the following order: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1-Jer.21.14">Jer 21:1-14</reference>, 34, 37, 32, 33, 38, 39. <div eID="gen29822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29823" type="x-p"/> Pashur the son of Melchiah - There can be little doubt that this Pashur was a different person from him who was called the son of Immur in the preceding chapter.
entries.36538bb5c9e1d7bf09248c695c81013ef4b9abe9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29824" type="x-p"/> Inquire, I pray thee - See whether God intends to deliver us into or out of the hand of the Chaldeans.
entries.4c789384b200db865ed62b493ebe3c422992911f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29825" type="x-p"/> I will turn back the weapons - Every attempt you make to repel the Chaldeans shall be unsuccessful. <div eID="gen29825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29826" type="x-p"/> I will assemble them into the midst of this city - I will deliver the city into their hands.
entries.a2d7e22121d18e2a019b3fbb390eefcef1d41e27: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29827" type="x-p"/> They shall die of a great pestilence - The sword may appear to be that of man, though I have given the Chaldeans their commission; but the pestilence shall appear to be the immediate act of God.
entries.151c29ef11a07a87ab63de75a4488c27571e9d73: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29828" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadrezzar - This name is spelt as above in twenty-six places of this book; and in ten places it is spelt Nebuchadnezzar, which is the common orthography. The difference is only a ר resh for a נ nun; but the MSS. are various on this point. It is the same person who is intended by both names; and here all the Versions, except the Arabic, which omits the name, have it in the usual form.
entries.b7ce8cf6ce83c45427c929e8d0754d52a7632342: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29829" type="x-p"/> Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death - Meaning escape or destruction in the present instance. This is explained in the next verse.
entries.b02be87c6c1f7883e8d589f98582e74fbbf165f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29830" type="x-p"/> He shall burn it with fire - What a heavy message to all; and especially to them who had any fear of God, or reverence for the temple and its sacred services!
entries.c91cc21493ed6794c253fd5c7ccf4450af5e19f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29831" type="x-p"/> Execute judgment in the morning - Probably the time for dispensing judgment was the morning, when the people were going to their work; but the words may mean, Do justice promptly, do not delay. Let justice be administered as soon as required.
entries.a24c4eec33a983607dc519d6fa9a487234b58566: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29832" type="x-p"/> O inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain - Dr. Blayney translates: "O thou inhabitant of the levelled hollow of a rock." With all his explanation I cannot see the good sense of this translation. Jerusalem itself, though partly on two hills, was also extended in the valley; and Zion, the city of David, was properly a rock, strongly fortified both by nature and art; and by its ancient possessors, the Jebusites, was deemed impregnable. <div eID="gen29832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29833" type="x-p"/> Who shall come down against us? - Probably the words of those courtiers who had persuaded Zedekiah to rebel against the king of Babylon.
entries.98d09852195e69e7d210115dd8bfef0021195284: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29834" type="x-p"/> I will kindle a fire in the forest thereof - I will send destruction into its center, that shall spread to every part of the circumference, and so consume the whole. <div eID="gen29834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29835" type="x-p"/> The beginning of the thirty-fourth chapter should follow here. See the arrangement on <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">Jer 34:1</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="Jer.21"/> <div eID="gen29835" type="x-p"/>

entries.317168dca1b817bbfb5b5bb3f7c64a37bd8d39f3: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference> <div eID="gen14088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14089" type="x-p"/> The Taking of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans. - <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference> and Jer 21:2. <hi type="italic">The heading specifying the occasion for the following prediction. "The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent unto him Pashur the son of Malchiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, saying: Inquire now of Jahveh for us, for Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon maketh war against us; if so be that the Lord will deal with us according to all His wondrous works, that he may go up from us."</hi> The fighting of Nebuchadrezzar is in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jer 21:4</reference> stated to be the besieging of the city. From this it appears that the siege had begun ere the king sent the two men to the prophet. Pashur the son of Malchiah is held by Hitz., Graf, Näg., etc., to be a distinguished priest of the class of Malchiah. But this is without sufficient reason; for he is not called a priest, as is the case with Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, and with Pashur the son of Immer (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>). Nor is anything proved by the circumstance that Pashur and Malchiah occur in several places as the names of priests, e.g., <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.12">1Ch 9:12</reference>; for both names are also used of persons not priests, e.g., Malchiah, Ezr 10:25, Ezr 10:31, and Pashur, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">Jer 38:1</reference>, where this son of Gedaliah is certainly a laic. From this passage, where Pashur ben Malchiah appears again, it is clear that the four men there named, who accused Jeremiah for his speech, were government authorities or court officials, since in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.4">Jer 38:4</reference> they are called שׂרים. Ros. is therefore right in saying of the Pashur under consideration: <hi type="italic">videtur unus ex principibus sive aulicis fuisse</hi>, cf. Jer 38:4. Only Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah is called priest; and he, acc. to <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">Jer 29:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jer 37:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24">Jer 52:24</reference>, held a high position in the priesthood. Inquire for us of Jahveh, i.e., ask for a revelation for us, as 2Ki 22:13, cf. Gen 25:22. It is not: pray for His help on our behalf, which is expressed by התפּלּל בּעדנוּ, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jer 37:3</reference>, cf. Jer 52:2. In the request for a revelation the element of intercession is certainly not excluded, but it is not directly expressed. But it is on this that the king founds his hope: Peradventure Jahveh will do with us (אותנוּ for אתּנוּ) according to all His wondrous works, i.e., in the miraculous manner in which He has so often saved us, e.g., under Hezekiah, and also, during the blockade of the city by Sennacherib, had recourse to the prophet Isaiah and besought his intercession with the Lord, 2Ki 19:2., Isa 37:2. That he (Nebuch.) may go up from us. עלה, to march against a city in order to besiege it or take it, but with מעל, to withdraw from it, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jer 37:5</reference>; 1Ki 15:19. As to the name Nebuchadrezzar, which corresponds more exactly than the Aramaic-Jewish Nebuchadnezzar with the <hi type="italic">Nebucadurriusur</hi> of the inscriptions (נבו כדר אצר, i.e., <hi type="italic">Nebo coronam servat</hi>), see <hi type="italic">Comm. on Daniel</hi> at Dan 1:1. <div eID="gen14089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14090" type="x-p"/> The Lord’s reply through Jeremiah consists of three parts: <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The answer to the king’s hope that the Lord will save Jerusalem from the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4-Jer.21.7">Jer 21:4-7</reference>); <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The counsel given to the people and the royal family as to how they may avert ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.8-Jer.21.12">Jer 21:8-12</reference>); <hi type="italic">c</hi>. The prediction that Jerusalem will be punished for her sins (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jer 21:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.21.14">Jer 21:14</reference>).
entries.0a0dd413afde09beb1a7c37c1abbd3ff2b0253ce: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.3-Jer.21.6">Jer 21:3-6</reference> <hi type="italic">The answer. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.3">Jer 21:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. "And Jeremiah said to them: Thus shall ye say to Zedekiah:</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jer 21:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. Thus hath Jahveh the God of Israel said: Behold, I turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands, wherewith ye fight against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans, which besiege you without the walls, and gather them together into the midst of this city.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.5">Jer 21:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, and with anger and fury and great wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.6">Jer 21:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. And smite the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast; of a great plague they shall die.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">Jer 21:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. And afterward, saith Jahveh, I will give Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his servants, and the people - namely, such as in this city are left of the plague, of the sword, and of the famine - into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those that seek after their life, that he may smite them according to the sharpness of the sword, not spare them, neither have pity nor mercy."</hi> This answer is intended to disabuse the king and his servants of all hope of help from God. So far from saving them from the Chaldeans, God will fight against them, will drive back into the city its defenders that are still holding out without the walls against the enemy; consume the inhabitants by sword, pestilence, famine; deliver the king, with his servants and all that survive inside the lines of the besiegers, into the hand of the latter, and unsparingly cause them to be put to death. "I make the weapons of war turn back" is carried on and explained by "I gather them into the city." The sense is: I will bring it about that ye, who still fight without the walls against the beleaguerers, must turn back with your weapons and retreat into the city. "Without the walls" is not to be joined to מסב, because this is too remote, and מחוּץ is by usage locative, not ablative. It should go with "wherewith ye fight," etc.: wherewith ye fight without the walls against the beleaguering enemies. The siege had but just begun, so that the Jews were still trying to hinder the enemy from taking possession of stronger positions and from a closer blockade of the city. In this they will not succeed, but their weapons will be thrust back into the city.
entries.0554ad54d8de290e5d945b9a4469cc932285e18d: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">Jer 21:7</reference> <div eID="gen14090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14091" type="x-p"/> The Lord will make known His almighty power not for the rescue but for the chastisement of Judah. The words "with outstretched hand and strong arm" are a standing figure for the miraculous manifestation of God’s power at the release of Israel from Egypt, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.15">Deu 5:15</reference>; Deu 26:8. This power He will now exercise upon Israel, and execute the punishment threatened against apostasy at the renewal of the covenant by Moses in the land of Moab. The words גּדול...בּאף are from Deu 29:27. The inhabitants of Jerusalem are to perish during the siege by pestilence and disease, and the remainder, including the king and his servants, to be mercilessly massacred. "Great pestilence" alone is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.6">Jer 21:6</reference>, but in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">Jer 21:7</reference> there are sword and famine along with it. The ואת before הנּשׁארים seems superfluous and unsuitable, since besides the king, his servants and the people, there could be none others left. The lxx have therefore omitted it, and Hitz., Ew., Graf, and others propose to erase it. But the ו may be taken to be explicative: namely, such as are left, in which case ואת serves to extend the participial clause to all the persons before mentioned, while without the ואת the 'הנּשׁארים וגו could be referred only to העם. "Into the hand of their enemies" is rhetorically amplified by "into the hand of those that seek," etc., as in <reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">Jer 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jer 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.20">Jer 34:20</reference>, etc.; לפי חרב, according to the sharpness (or edge) of the sword, i.e., mercilessly (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.34.26">Gen 34:26</reference>; in Jer. only here), explained by "not spare them," etc., cf. Jer 13:14.
entries.791aa829b7d03cc5f04f55f5315197bbdeedee6d: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.8-Jer.21.10">Jer 21:8-10</reference> <hi type="italic">The counsel given to the people and royal family how to escape death. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.8">Jer 21:8</reference> <hi type="italic">. "And unto the people thou shalt say: Thus hath Jahveh said: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jer 21:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. He that abideth in this city shall die by sword, by famine, and by pestilence; but he that goeth out and falleth to the Chaldeans that besiege you, he shall live, and have his soul for a prey.</hi> Jer 21:10. <hi type="italic">For I have set my face on this city for evil and not for good, saith Jahveh; into the hand of the king of Babylon shall it be given, who shall burn it with fire.</hi> Jer 21:11. <hi type="italic">And to the house of the king of Judah: Hear the word of Jahveh:</hi> Jer 21:12. <hi type="italic">House of David! thus hath Jahveh said: Hold judgment every morning, and save the despoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, lest my fury break forth as fire, and burn unquenchably, because of the evil of your doings."</hi> What the prophet is here to say to the people and the royal house is not directly addressed to the king’s envoy, but is closely connected with the answer he was to give to the latter, and serves to strengthen the same. We need not be hampered by the assumption that Jeremiah, immediately after that answer, communicated this advice, so that it might be made known to the people and to the royal house. The counsel given in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.8-Jer.21.12">Jer 21:8-12</reference> to the people was during the siege repeatedly given by Jeremiah both to the king and to the people, cf. Jer 38:1., Jer 38:17., and Jer 27:11., and many of the people acted by his advice, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">Jer 38:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>; Jer 52:15. But the defenders of the city, the authorities, saw therein treason, or at least a highly dangerous discouragement to those who were fighting, and accused the prophet as a traitor, Jer 38:4., cf. Jer 37:13. Still Jeremiah, holding his duty higher than his life, remained in the city, and gave as his opinion, under conviction attained to only by divine revelation, that all resistance is useless, since God has irrevocably decreed the destruction of Jerusalem as a punishment for their sins. The idea of <reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">Jer 21:7</reference> is clothed in words taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.30.15">Deu 30:15</reference>, cf. Deu 11:26. ישׁב , <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jer 21:9</reference>, as opposed to יצא, does not mean: to dwell, but: to sit still, abide. To fall to the Chaldeans, i.e., to go over to them, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.37.14">Jer 37:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>; 2Ki 25:11; על is interchanged with אל, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.13">Jer 37:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">Jer 38:19</reference>; Jer 52:15. The <hi type="italic">Chet</hi>. יחיה is right, corresponding to ימוּת; the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> וחיה is wrong. His life shall be to him for a prey, i.e., he shall carry it thence as a prey, i.e., preserve it. <reference osisRef="Jer.21.10">Jer 21:10</reference> gives the reason for the advice given. For I have set my face, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.44.11">Jer 44:11</reference>, recalls <reference osisRef="Amos.9.4">Amo 9:4</reference>, only there we have עיני for פּני, as in Jer 24:6. To set the face or eye on one means: to pay special heed to him, in good (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.39.12">Jer 39:12</reference>) or in evil sense; hence the addition, "for evil," etc.
entries.b04261666a2af80bbb15894d525dbcf69f98e669: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.11-Jer.21.12">Jer 21:11-12</reference><note placement="foot">According to Hitz., Gr., and Näg., the passage <reference osisRef="Jer.21.11-Jer.21.14">Jer 21:11-14</reference> stands in no inner connection with the foregoing, and may, from the contents of it, be seen to belong to an earlier period than that of the siege which took place under Zedekiah, namely, to the time of Jehoiakim, because, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. in the period of Jer 21:1. such an exhortation and conditional threatening must have been out of place after their destruction had been quite unconditionally foretold to Zedekiah and the people in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4-Jer.21.7">Jer 21:4-7</reference>; <hi type="italic">b</hi>. the defiant tone conveyed in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jer 21:13</reference> is inconsistent with the cringing despondency shown by Zedekiah in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jer 21:2</reference>; <hi type="italic">c</hi>. it is contrary to what we would expect to find the house of the king addressed separately after the king had been addressed in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.3">Jer 21:3</reference>, the king being himself comprehended in his "house." But these arguments, on which Hitz. builds ingenious hypotheses, are perfectly valueless. As to <hi type="italic">a</hi>, we have to remark: In <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4-Jer.21.7">Jer 21:4-7</reference> unconditional destruction is foretold against neither king nor people; it is only said that the Chaldeans will capture the city - that the inhabitants will be smitten with pestilence, famine, and sword - and that the king, with his servants and those that are left, will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, who will smite them unsparingly. But in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jer 21:12</reference> the threatening is uttered against the king, that if he does not practise righteousness, the wrath of God will be kindled unquenchably, and, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.14">Jer 21:14</reference>, that Jerusalem is to be burnt with fire. In <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4-Jer.21.7">Jer 21:4-7</reference> there is no word of the burning of the city; it is first threatened, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.10">Jer 21:10</reference>, against the people, after the choice has been given them of escaping utter destruction. How little the burning of Jerusalem is involved in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4-Jer.21.7">Jer 21:4-7</reference> may be seen from the history of the siege and capture of Jerusalem under Jehoiachin, on which occasion, too, the king, with his servants and the people, was given into the hand of the king of Babylon, while the city was permitted to stand, and the deported king remained in life, and was subsequently set free from his captivity by Evil-Merodach. But that Zedekiah, by hearkening to the word of the Lord, can alleviate his doom and save Jerusalem from destruction, this Jeremiah tells him yet later in very plain terms, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17-Jer.38.23">Jer 38:17-23</reference>, cf. Jer 34:4. Lastly, the release of Hebrew man-servants and maid-servants, recounted in Jer 34:8., shows that even during the siege there were cases of an endeavour to turn and follow the law, and consequently that an exhortation to hold by the right could not have been regarded as wholly superfluous. - The other two arguments, <hi type="italic">b</hi> and <hi type="italic">c</hi>, are totally inconclusive. How the confidence of the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the strength of its fortifications (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jer 21:13</reference>) is contradictory of the fact related in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jer 21:2</reference>, does not appear. That Zedekiah should betake himself to the prophet, desiring him to entreat the help of God, is not a specimen of cringing despondency such as excludes all confidence in any earthly means of help. Nor are defiance and despondency mutually exclusive opposites in psychological experience, but states of mind that rapidly alternate. Finally, Näg. seems to have added the last argument (c) only because he had no great confidence in the two others, which had been dwelt on by Hitz. and Graf. Why should not Jeremiah have given the king another counsel for warding off the worst, over and above that conveyed in the answer to his question (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4-Jer.21.7">Jer 21:4-7</reference>)? - These arguments have therefore not pith enough to throw any doubt on the connection between the two passages (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.8-Jer.21.10">Jer 21:8-10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.21.11">Jer 21:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jer 21:12</reference>) indicated by the manner in which "and to the house (וּלבית) of the king of Judah" points back to "and unto this people thou shalt say" (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.8">Jer 21:8</reference>), or to induce us to attribute the connection so indicated to the thoughtlessness of the editor.</note> <div eID="gen14091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14092" type="x-p"/> The kingly house, i.e., the king and his family, under which are here comprehended not merely women and children, but also the king’s companions, his servants and councillors; they are counselled to hold judgment every morning. דּין משׁפּט = דּין דּין, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.28">Jer 5:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">Jer 22:16</reference>, or שׁפט, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.59">Lam 3:59</reference>; 1Ki 3:28. לבּקר distributively, every morning, as Amo 4:4. To save the despoiled out of the hand of the oppressor means: to defend his just cause against the oppressor, to defend him from being despoiled; cf. Jer 22:3. The form of address; House of David, which is by a displacement awkwardly separated from שׁמעוּ, is meant to remind the kingly house of its origin, its ancestor David, who walked in the ways of the Lord. - The second half of the verse, "lest my fury," etc., runs like Jer 4:4.
entries.35af4761b39706b69e03ecb62f372cb13c48f21a: <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13-Jer.21.14">Jer 21:13-14</reference> <hi type="italic">The chastisement of Jerusalem. -</hi> Jer 21:13. <hi type="italic">"Behold, I am against thee, inhabitress of the valley, of the rock of the plain, saith Jahveh, ye who say: Who shall come down against us, and who shall come into our dwellings?</hi> Jer 21:14. <hi type="italic">And will visit you according to the fruit of your doings, saith Jahveh, and kindle a fire in her forest, that it may devour all her surroundings."</hi> This threatening is levelled against the citizens of Jerusalem, who vaunted the impregnableness of their city. The inhabitress of the valley is the daughter of Zion, the population of Jerusalem personified. The situation of the city is spoken of as עמק, ravine between mountains, in respect that Jerusalem was encircled by mountains of greater height (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference>); and as rock of the plain, i.e., the region regarded as a level from which Mount Zion, the seat of the kingdom, rose, equivalent to rock of the field, Jer 17:3. In the "rock" we think specially of Mount Zion, and in the "valley" of the so-called lower city. The two designations are chosen to indicate the strong situation of Jerusalem. On this the inhabitants pride themselves, who say: Who shall come down against us? יחת for ינחת, from נחת; cf. Ew. §139, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. Dwellings, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jer 25:30</reference>, not cities or refuge or coverts of wild animals; מעון has not this force, but can at most acquire it from the context; see Del. on Psa 26:8. The strength of the city will not shield the inhabitants from the punishment with which God will visit them. "According to the fruit," etc., cf. Jer 17:10. I kindle fire in her forest. The city is a forest of houses, and the figure is to be explained by the simile in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.6">Jer 22:6</reference>, but was not suggested by מעון = <hi type="italic">lustra ferarum</hi> (Hitz.). All her surroundings, how much more then the city itself! Rebuke of the Ungodly Kings Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin, and Promise of a Righteous Branch of David. - This discourse begins with an exhortation to the king, his servants, and the people to do right and justice, and to eschew all unrighteousness, and with the warning, that in case of the contrary the royal palace will be reduced to ruins and Jerusalem destroyed by fire. After touching briefly on the fate of Jehoahaz, who has been deported to Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.10-Jer.22.12">Jer 22:10-12</reference>), the discourse turns against Jehoiakim, rebukes his tyranny, in that he builds his house with unrighteousness and schemes only bloodshed and violence, and threatens him with ignominious ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.19">Jer 22:13-19</reference>). Then, after a threatening against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.20-Jer.22.23">Jer 22:20-23</reference>), it deals with Jechoniah, who is told he shall be carried to Babylon never to return, and without any descendant to sit on his throne (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.24-Jer.22.30">Jer 22:24-30</reference>). Next, after an outcry of grief at the wicked shepherds, follows the promise that the Lord will gather the remnant of His flock out of all the lands whither they have been driven, that He will restore them to their fields and multiply them, and that He will raise up to them a good shepherd in the righteous branch of David (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.1-Jer.23.8">Jer 23:1-8</reference>). - According to <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jer 21:1</reference>, Jeremiah spoke these words in the house of the king of Judah; whence we see that in this passage we have not merely ideas and scraps of addresses gathered together, such as had been on various occasions orally delivered by the prophet. It further appears from <reference osisRef="Jer.22.10">Jer 22:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.17">Jer 22:13-17</reference>, that the portion of the discourse addressed to Jehoiakim was uttered in the first year of his reign; and from <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jer 22:24</reference>, where Jechoniah is addressed as king, that the utterance concerning him belongs to the short period (only three months long) of his reign. But the utterance concerning Jechoniah is joined with that concerning Jehoiakim on account of the close relationship in matter between them. The exhortation and warning against injustice, forming the introduction, as regards it contents, fits very well into the time of Jehoiakim (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.22.17">Jer 22:17</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jer 22:3</reference>). The promise with which the discourse concludes was apparently not spoken till the time of Jechoniah, shortly before his being taken to Babylon. So that we have here the discourses of Jeremiah belonging to the times of Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin respectively, joined into one continuous whole.  <chapter eID="Jer.21"/> <div eID="gen14092" type="x-p"/>

entries.3243efbce4d495eae9cb8bf044241af9e40a2a20: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.21.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.21.1" sID="gen57738" type="section"/> <div sID="gen57739" type="x-p"/>Jeremiah relates how he received the king’s messengers, who sought from him an answer, whether he could bring any comfort in a state of things so perplexed and almost hopeless, he then says, that two had been sent to him; one was Pashur, not the priest mentioned in the last chapter, for he was the son of Immer but this was the son of Melchiah; and the other was Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah. But he shews that the king and his counsellors were disappointed of their hope, for they expected a favor-able answer, as though God would be propitious to Jerusalem; but the Prophet answered as he was commanded by God, that it was all over with the city, the kingdom, and the whole nation.<div eID="gen57739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen57740" type="x-p"/>We shall also see from other passages that Zedekiah was not one of the worst; though he did not really fear God and was led away by false counsels, there was yet in him some regard for religion, so that he did not avowedly despise God as Epicureans do. Many such are found even at this day in the world, who think it enough to cherish a half-buried fear of God, and to retain some little regard for religion; but it is very fading, and disappears on even the least occasion. So it was with Zedekiah; he was as it were neutral, for he neither seriously worshipped God nor yet despised him.<div eID="gen57740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen57741" type="x-p"/>Hence it was, that he sent messengers to Jeremiah. He knew that while God was displeased with them no safety could be hoped for; but he did not understand the way of appeasing God, nor had he any real desire to be reconciled to him; as the case is with hypocrites, who, though they wish God to be kind to them, yet when God’s mercy is offered to them, either openly reject it, or are unwilling to embrace it, because they cannot bear to surrender themselves to God. Such was the state of mind in which Zedekiah was; and hence it was, that he asked the Prophet to consult God. But we must also observe that this was an honorable message; and it hence more fully appears that Zedekiah was not one of those furious tyrants, who like the giants seek to fight with God. For by sending two messengers to the Prophet, and employing him as an advocate to seek some favor from God, he proved that religion was not wholly suppressed and extinguished in him.<div eID="gen57741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen57742" type="x-p"/>And hence also it may be seen how bold and courageous was the Prophet; for he was not softened by the honor paid to him, but gave such answer as was calculated to exasperate the king, and to drive him into great rage. But we ought especially to notice, that they did not flatter the Prophet so as to induce him to give a false answer, but wished God to be consulted. It hence appears that they were convinced of Jeremiah’s integrity, that he would say nothing rashly or from himself, but would be a faithful interpreter and herald of heavenly oracles. And yet we see, and shall hereafter see in several passages, that the king was very incensed against God’s Prophet. But hypocrites, though they are forced to reverence God, are yet carried here and there, and maintain no consistency, especially when they perceive that God is against them; for they are not turned by threatenings. They cannot, therefore, but make tumult, and strive like refractory horses to shake off their rider. Such an instance we find in Zedekiah; for he acknowledged Jeremiah as God’s faithful servant; for he did not say, “Tell a lie for us, or in our favor but, <hi type="italic">inquire of God for us.</hi><div eID="gen57742" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.21.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen57738" osisID="Jer.21.1" type="section"/>
entries.b0355756cd19a0870e07d88e6e42e4d2e064a530: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.21.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.21.2" sID="gen57743" type="section"/> <div sID="gen57744" type="x-p"/>He then adds, <hi type="italic">If Jehovah will deal with us according to all his wondrous works</hi> <note n="19"> <div sID="gen57745" type="x-p"/> The “if” may better be rendered “it may be,” <foreign xml:lang="he">אולי</foreign>; it is so rendered by the Vulg., Syr., and the Targ. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen57745" type="x-p"/> </note> We again see that Zedekiah had some sense of religion; but it was very evanescent; for he was not influenced by any real impression, being like hypocrites who wish, as it has been said, to have peace with God, provided it be on their own terms. But as they are unwilling wholly to surrender themselves to God, they take a circuituous course, and seek to allure God to themselves, at least they come not to him except through various windings, and not in a direct way. Hence Zedekiah refers here to God’s miraculous works which had been wrought in behalf of the Israelites in all ages; as though he had said, “God has hitherto dealt; in a wonderful manner with his chosen people, and whenever he brought help to our fathers, he manifested wonderful proofs of his power; will he not deal with us at this day in the same manner?” He assumes the principle, that God’s covenant remained inviolable; and this was quite true, but the application was false; for Zedekiah and the whole people ought to have kept faith with God. For if they wished God to be propitious to them, why did they not in return worship and serve him as their God? But as they were covenant-breakers, how foolishly and vainly did they allege God’s covenant, which they themselves had rendered void? But it is usual with hypocrites to apply to themselves every favor which God shews to his own children; for they falsely assume the name as a covering, and say, that they are members of the Church because God had adopted them. This was the reason why Zedekiah asked whether God would do according to his wonderful works, as though he had said, “Surely God is ever like himself, and we are his people; and as he has so often delivered his Church, and in such various ways, his power has always been wonderfully displayed; why, then, will he not deal with us in the same manner?”<div eID="gen57744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen57746" type="x-p"/>He at last, adds, <hi type="italic">that he may ascend from us</hi>, <note n="20"> <div sID="gen57747" type="x-p"/> The Syr. Renders the verb “ascend” as a Hiphil; and more consistently with the passage, “and drive him away from us.” With the exception of the Arab., the Versions and the Targ. Render the first verb in the verse, not “inquire,” but “ask,” or “pray the Lord for us.” Then the verse would be as follows: —<div eID="gen57747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen57748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> Pray now for us to Jehovah; for Nebuchadrezzar, the king of Babylon, is warring against us: it may be that Jehovah will deal with us according to all his wondrous works, and make him to depart from us.<div eID="gen57748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen57749" type="x-p"/>The verb <foreign xml:lang="he">דרש</foreign>, transitively as here, means to seek: see <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.34.5">Psalm 34:5</reference>. And to seek the favor of Jehovah, or to pray to him, seems most consistent with the latter part of the verse. Blayney’s rendering is, “Intreat, we pray thee, Jehovah for us;” and this is the meaning taken by Venema and Gataker. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen57749" type="x-p"/> </note> that is, that the King Nebuchadnezzar may raise the siege and leave us free.<div eID="gen57746" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.21.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen57743" osisID="Jer.21.2" type="section"/>
entries.cf28596f3a613922f0cb57e19e4b25a6e92ebe0f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.21.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.21.3" sID="gen57750" type="section"/> <div sID="gen57751" type="x-p"/>Now follows the answer of Jeremiah, <hi type="italic">say ye to Zedekiah, </hi>etc.; he did not go to the king himself, but by way of contempt delivered the message to be borne by the messengers. The Prophet no doubt did this designedly, and through the impulse of the Holy Spirit. He did not, indeed, proudly despise his king; but it was necessary for him by his magnanimity to cast down the pride of the king, so that he might know that he had to do with the living God, whom he had very insolently treated. <hi type="italic">Say ye to Zedekiah, Thus saith Jehovah, the God of Israel, </hi>etc. He adds the words, <hi type="italic">the God of Israel, </hi>that Zedekiah might know that the wonderful works, in reliance on which he still thought that their condition was safe, did not belong to him and the people; as though the Prophet had said, “Though God did not help thee and thy people, he would not yet be inconsistent with himself, or depart from his covenant; but he would remain ever the God of Israel, though he destroyed thee and all thy people.”<div eID="gen57751" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.21.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen57750" osisID="Jer.21.3" type="section"/>
entries.26608f4103af412aace111c3596c70b4e91d756f:
He says, Behold I, etc.; it was said before, Nebuchadnezzar is come to make war with us: now he says, “I am God;” as though he had said, “Nebuchadnezzar may be conquered, he may change his counsel, he may leave you through weariness; but know ye that Nebuchadnezzar fights under my authority.” Behold, he says, I prohibit (for so ought מסכ to be rendered) all the warlike instruments which are in your hands, and with which ye fight against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans; as though he had said, “However furnished ye may be with weapons and forces, and whatever may be necessary to defend the city, I forbid the use of these weapons, that is, I will cause that they will avail you nothing.” Some, as I have said, render the word, “I will turn them against you.” But the meaning seems more suitable to the etymology of the word, when we say, that the weapons which the Jews had would avail them nothing, because God would prevent them from producing any effect.
The verb סכ means to turn, to turn aside, to turn round, to change; it seems to mean here to turn to a contrary purpose, to turn from the right use, to divert, to revert, or to reverse, “Behold, I will reverse the instruments of war which are in your hands; μετάστρεφω — I change,” that is, to what is opposite, is the Sept.; Blayney reads, “Behold, I will turn aside,” etc. — Ed
He afterwards adds, the Chaldeans, who fight without the wall against you He described their state at that time, for the city was besieged by the Chaldeans; there was a wall between them, and the Jews thought that they could repel the attacks of their enemies. But God says, “the Chaldeans are this day shut out by the wall, but I will gather them, he says, into the middle of this city; that is, I will make a breach, so that the wall may not be a hinderance to prevent, the Chaldeans from occupying the very bosom of the city.” It follows, —
Jeremiah 21:5
5. And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in fury, and in great wrath.
5. Et praeliabor ego contra vos in manu extenta et brachio robusto, et in ira et furore et excandescentia magna.
entries.36bec4f4224dd780c231032efb318dfcf5023d3c:
He proceeds with the subject; and though he afterwards is more diffuse, he yet confirms here what we have just seen, — even that God was the leader of the war, and that the Chaldeans were, as it were, his hired soldiers, whom he guided by his own hand, and to whom he would give the signal to fight.
I, myself he says, will fight against you He put this in opposition to the wonderful works which Zedekiah had mentioned. God, indeed, had formerly been in a wonderful way present with his Church, not only once, but a thousand times; but he says now, “whatever power I have, it shall be exercised now against you; expect, therefore, no aid from me, but know that I am armed, and shall wholly destroy you.” He adds, with an extended hand and a strong arm; as though he had said, “your fathers found wonderful works done for their safety; but you shall by experience learn how great is my power to destroy you.” In short, he means that all God’s power would be a cause of terror to the Jews, and that therefore they could not escape, as there is nothing more dreadful than to have God’s hand opposed to us. To the same purpose is what follows, in wrath, and in fury, and in great indignation
There seems to be a gradation in these terms, — “in wrath, and in hot displeasure, and in great foaming indignation.” The first word means simply wrath or anger; the second, heated wrath; and the third, foaming wrath, and “great” is added to it.
